extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students studying real analysis / Fourier series (French-language)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria for (1) developing a function as a trigonometric (Fourier) series: orthogonality, computation of coefficients, endpoint behavior, termwise integration/differentiation, and graphical representation; and (2) deciding convergence/divergence of improper definite integrals where the differential element becomes infinite (endpoint or interior singularities) using power-law/comparison tests and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for development in trigonometric series (développement en série trigonométrique)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function f(x) is finite and continuous on an interval [a,b] (mapped to [−π,+π] if desired by change of variable), it can be developed, for x in that open interval, into a convergent trigonometric series of the form f(x)=a0 + Σ (an cos nx + bn sin nx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may simplify by changing variable to map [a,b] to [−π,+π]. The expansion is valid for x strictly between the endpoints; at the endpoints the series takes a single value (see endpoint/limit rule). Integrating the series term-by-term yields a convergent series whose sum is an antiderivative of f in the same interval. However, differentiating term-by-term is not guaranteed to produce a convergent series (example given where derivatives lead to non-vanishing general term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality integrals used to determine Fourier coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The integrals ∫_{−π}^{π} cos m x cos n x dx and ∫_{−π}^{π} sin m x sin n x dx vanish for m≠n; ∫_{−π}^{π} sin m x cos n x dx = 0. Also ∫_{−π}^{π} cos^2 n x dx = ∫_{−π}^{π} sin^2 n x dx = π for n≠0 (and special values when n=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using these orthogonality relations, multiply the assumed series by cos nx or sin nx and integrate over −π..π: all cross-terms vanish leaving the coefficient term. Thus the coefficients are given by integrals of f times cos nx or sin nx (a_n and b_n are proportional to the mean values of f(x)cos nx and f(x)sin nx in the interval), and a0 is the average (mean) value of f on the interval. The text gives the explicit integrals and explains the factors (e.g. a_n equals twice the mean of f(x)cos nx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula / interpretation of coefficients (a0, an, bn)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant term a0 is the mean value of f on the interval; the coefficients an and bn are proportional to the mean values of f(x)cos nx and f(x)sin nx respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute by multiplying the series by cos nx or sin nx and integrating over the interval: only the matching harmonic survives. The text emphasizes that knowing the mean values ∫ f, ∫ f cos nx, ∫ f sin nx for n≥1 determines the trigonometric development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of series at a discontinuity / endpoint (limit rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the endpoints (or at a point of discontinuity), the Fourier (trigonometric) series converges to a single value equal to the average (arithmetical mean) of the left and right limits of the function at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The development is valid and equals f(x) for x strictly inside the interval. At the two limiting values (the endpoints) the series takes the same value (the average). The book discusses that the sum need not equal f(±π) but equals the mean of the lateral values when discontinuities occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-by-term integration and differentiation of trigonometric series
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrating a convergent trigonometric series term-by-term produces a convergent series whose sum is an antiderivative of f on the same interval. Differentiation term-by-term is not always permitted — the derived series may diverge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Differentiating a sine-series termwise produces cosine terms whose general term does not tend to zero, hence the derived series can diverge. The text gives an explicit example showing divergence of the derivative-series and warns against unjustified termwise differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and properties of polynomial sequence P_n (basis with mean-value properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a sequence of polynomials P_0, P_1, ..., P_n on [−h,+h] with properties: P_0 = 1; for μ>0, P_μ' = P_{μ−1}; and the mean value of each P_μ (for μ≥1) over the interval is zero. These polynomials form a basis for expressing polynomials via mean-values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties uniquely determine the polynomials; the text shows how to compute the first ones and summarizes their mean-value table. They are used to express any polynomial f of degree p as f(x)=Σ a_k P_k(x), where the coefficients a_k equal mean values of derivatives of f (so a_k = mean of f^{(k)}). This yields formula (3) expressing a polynomial in terms of mean values of f and its derivatives over the interval; as h→0 this reduces to the Maclaurin formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of mean-value polynomial expansion to general functions — caution
rubrics_metrics.description: By analogy the polynomial formula can be extended formally to a function admitting derivatives of all orders on [−h,h]: f(x)=Σ (mean of f^{(k)}) P_k(x), but this series is not generally convergent or applicable to all functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: for pure trigonometric functions (e.g. A_v sin v x + B_v cos v x with integer v), all mean-values vanish, making the series trivial and inapplicable. The text notes the formula may be useful in practice but is exact only in special, hard-to-characterize cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of improper definite integral when differential element becomes infinite at endpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: When f(x) is finite on [a,b) but becomes infinite at x=b, define the improper integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx as the limit as ε→0+ of ∫_a^{b−ε} f(x) dx. If the limit exists finite the integral 'converges' (has a value); if the limit → +∞ (or −∞) the integral 'diverges' (is infinite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: area under curve up to an asymptote. Two cases: finite limit gives finite area between curve and asymptote; infinite limit means infinite area. Examples illustrate both behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-law test for integrals with singularity of form (b−x)^{−n}
rubrics_metrics.description: The improper integral ∫_a^b (b−x)^{−n} dx (with n>0) converges (finite) iff n<1 and diverges (infinite) iff n≥1. For n=1 the antiderivative is −log(b−x) and the integral diverges as ε→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute ∫_{a}^{b−ε} (b−x)^{−n} dx = ( (b−a)^{1−n} − ε^{1−n} )/(1−n) for n≠1; examine ε→0. The text works out the algebra and the special n=1 case explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison/comparable-product test using (b−x)^n f(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists n<1 such that (b−x)^n f(x) → L (finite) as x→b, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx converges. If there exists n≥1 such that (b−x)^n f(x) → L ≠ 0 as x→b, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea in text: split integral at c close to b; bound (b−x)^n f(x) by a constant M near b when n<1 and reduce to ∫ (b−x)^{−n} which converges when n<1. If n≥1 and limit nonzero, the function is asymptotically ≥ const⋅(b−x)^{-n} with n≥1 so the integral diverges. The text provides worked examples applying this test (including logarithmic and oscillatory examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of singularity at interior point (split-interval rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the integrand becomes infinite at some interior point c ∈ (a,b), the integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx is defined by splitting into two improper integrals ∫_a^c f(x) dx + ∫_c^b f(x) dx; the full integral exists only if both pieces exist (are finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate that one side may converge while the other diverges (making total integral divergent), or both may converge giving a finite total area; symmetric/asymmetric cases are discussed. The book warns against applying ordinary definite-integral rules when singularities are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign-preserving singularities: same conclusions apply
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x) tends to ±∞ while preserving sign as x→b (or x→a), the same power-law and comparison conclusions hold: existence of n<1 with (b−x)^n f(x) bounded → convergence; if n≥1 and limit nonzero → divergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text observes one can reduce the negative-sign case to the positive by changing sign of function or orientation; proofs and examples are analogous to the positive case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worked-example guidance and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing improper integrals, compute the local asymptotic behavior near the singularity and compare with standard model integrals (b−x)^{−n} or logarithmic cases; do not naively apply indefinite integrals across singularities without limit-taking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives several examples: ∫ (b−x)^{-1/2} converges; ∫ (b−x)^{-1} diverges (log); ∫ log x / sqrt x near 0 treated by choosing an exponent n and showing boundedness; ∫ dx/(1−x)^{1} type behavior diverges; warns that directly evaluating the antiderivative at the singular endpoint without limit is 'absurde'. Use splitting at interior singularities and check each side.
